items.title: Section: The Condition of Immediate Succession — Why the Mind Endlessly Yields Its Seat to the Mind That Follows

items.zh: 復次，云何等無間緣？謂此諸心心所無間，彼諸心心所生，說此為彼等無間緣。若此六識為彼六識等無間緣，即施設此名為意根，亦名意處、亦名意界。
items.en:
The Chapter of Deciding Discernment on the Five Sense-Consciousness-Corresponding Ground and the Mind Ground, part two.
Second, the condition of immediate succession; first, the question posed. Furthermore, what is the condition of immediate succession?
Second, the explanation; first, stating its meaning. Whenever these minds and mental factors have ceased without gap, and those minds and mental factors thereupon arise, the former are called the condition of immediate succession for the latter.
Second, identifying the six consciousnesses. If these six consciousnesses serve as the condition of immediate succession for those six consciousnesses that follow, this very set is thereby designated the mental faculty, also called the mental sense-base, also called the mental element.

items.title: Section: The Condition of the Perceived Object, and the First Two of Six Kinds of Dominant Condition

items.zh: 云何所緣緣？謂五識身，以色等五境，如其次第為所緣緣。若意識，以一切內外十二處為所緣緣。云何增上緣？謂眼等處，為眼識等俱生增上緣。若作意於所緣境，為諸識引發增上緣。
items.en:
Third, the condition of the perceived object; first, the question posed. What is the condition of the perceived object? Second, the explanation; first, the five sense-consciousness bodies. For the five sense-consciousness bodies, form and the rest of the five objects serve, each in its proper order, as their condition of the perceived object. Second, mental consciousness. For mental consciousness, all twelve internal and external sense-bases serve as its condition of the perceived object.
Fourth, the condition of dominant influence; first, the question posed. What is the condition of dominant influence? Second, the explanation; first, the co-arising dominant condition. The eye and the rest of the sense-bases serve as the co-arising dominant condition for eye-consciousness and the rest.
Second, the inducing dominant condition. If attention is directed towards the perceived object, it serves as the inducing dominant condition for the consciousnesses.

items.title: Section: Four More Kinds of Dominant Condition — Karma's Quiet Ledger, and Master Wùdá's Face-Sore of Pride

items.zh: 若諸心心所，展轉互為俱生增上緣。若淨不淨業，與後愛非愛果及異熟果，為先所作增上緣。若田、糞水等，與諸苗稼，為成辦增上緣。若彼彼工巧智，與彼彼世間工巧業處，為工業增上緣。
items.en:
Third, the mutual dominant condition. Mind and its mental factors serve reciprocally as each other's co-arising dominant condition.
Fourth, the previously-accomplished dominant condition. Pure or impure karma serves as the dominant condition, previously accomplished, for a later desired or undesired result and its ripened fruit.
Fifth, the condition that brings a result to completion. A field together with manure and water serves as the dominant condition bringing crops and seedlings to completion.
Sixth, the dominant condition of skilled craft. This or that craft-knowledge serves as the dominant condition for this or that worldly craft-activity.

items.title: Section: Only One of Four Conditions Truly Generates — The Rest Are Merely Instrumental, and Why All Phenomena Never Arise at Once

items.zh: 復次，是四緣中，因緣一種望所生法，能為生因，餘三種緣望所生法，當知但為方便因。是故彼彼諸行生方便緣現在前時，彼彼諸行種子便能生起彼彼諸行，是故諸行無有同時頓生起義。當知依止如是四緣建立十因，如菩薩地等中已說。
items.en:
Third, clarifying their subsumption; first, subsumed by two causes; first, stating the distinction; first, the generative cause. Furthermore, among these four conditions, the causal condition alone, in relation to the phenomenon it produces, is the generative cause.
Second, the instrumental cause. The remaining three conditions, in relation to the phenomenon produced, should be known as merely instrumental causes.
Second, explaining how they serve as condition. Therefore, only when the instrumental conditions for this or that conditioned phenomenon are actually present before it does the seed of this or that phenomenon give rise to it — therefore conditioned phenomena never have the meaning of arising all together at once.
Second, subsumed by the ten causes. One should know that, in reliance on these four conditions, the ten causes are established, as already explained in the Bodhisattva Stage and elsewhere.

items.title: Section: Reconciling Scripture — How Mental Consciousness Alone Can Take Even a Non-Existent Past or Future as Its Object

items.zh: 問：如世尊言：過去諸行為緣生意，未來諸行為緣生意。過去、未來諸行非有，何故世尊宣說彼行為緣生意？若意亦緣非有事境而得生者，云何不違微妙言說？如世尊言：由二種緣諸識得生。何等為二？謂眼及色，如是廣說乃至意、法。答：由能執持諸五識身所不行義，故佛世尊假說名法。是故說言：緣意及法，意識得生。
items.en:
Third, reconciling with scriptural statements; first, the meaning of mind taking the non-existent as object; first, a brief explanation of the hidden intention; first, the first question and answer; first, the question; first, raising the intended meaning. Question: as the Blessed One said, past conditioned phenomena serve as condition giving rise to mental consciousness, and future conditioned phenomena serve as condition giving rise to mental consciousness — since past and future conditioned phenomena are not existent, why does the Blessed One teach that these phenomena serve as condition giving rise to mental consciousness?
Second, raising the apparent contradiction; first, redirecting the question. If mental consciousness can indeed arise by taking a non-existent thing as its object, how does this not contradict the subtle teaching? Second, citing scriptural proof. As the Blessed One said, consciousness of every kind arises through two conditions. What are the two? The eye and form, and so on in full detail up through mental faculty and phenomena.
Second, the answer. Answer: because mental consciousness is capable of taking hold of what the five sense-consciousness bodies themselves cannot engage, the Blessed One provisionally applied the name "phenomena" to this scope. Therefore it is said: by taking mind and phenomena as condition, mental consciousness arises.

items.title: Section: Why We Know This Is the Buddha's Real Intention — Empirically Available, Yet Never Substantially Real

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，知佛世尊有是密意？答：由彼意識亦緣去來識為境界世現可得，非彼境識法處所攝。
items.en:
Second, the second question and answer; first, the question. Question: for what reason does one know the Blessed One holds this hidden intention?
Second, the answer; first, the explanation; first, stating what it is subsumed under. Answer: because mental consciousness does indeed take past and future consciousness-related events as its object, this being empirically available in the world — yet that object-event is not subsumed under the category of substantially real phenomena belonging to the sense-base of mental objects.

items.title: Section: Why "Phenomena" Covers Both the Real and the Unreal — And the First Reasoning: Contemplating No-Self

items.zh: 又有性者，安立有義、能持有義；若無性者，安立無義、能持無義；故皆名法。由彼意識，於有性義，若由此義而得安立，即以此義起識了別。於無性義，若由此義而得安立，即以此義起識了別。若於二種不由二義起了別者，不應說意緣一切義、取一切義。設作是說，便應違害自悉彈多。又不應言：如其所有，非有亦爾，是如理說。是故意識，如去來事非實有相，緣彼為境。由此故知意識亦緣非有為境。復有廣大言論道理，由此證知有緣無識。謂如世尊微妙言說：若內、若外及二中間都無有我。此我無性，非有為攝、非無為攝，共相觀識非不緣彼境界而轉。此名第一言論
items.en:
Second, clarifying this statement; first, explaining the name "phenomena." Whatever possesses existent nature is established as having the meaning of existence, capable of being held as such; whatever lacks existent nature is established as having the meaning of non-existence, capable of being held as such — therefore both are called phenomena.
Second, extensively discussing the reasoning; first, stating it. There is furthermore an extensive body of reasoning by which one may confirm that there is indeed a consciousness that takes the non-existent as its object.
Second, the explanation; first, presenting five reasonings; first, distinguishing them; first, the reasoning that establishes selflessness. As the Blessed One's subtle teaching states: there is no self to be found whether within, without, or in between the two. This self has no nature at all, subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned. The consciousness that contemplates this shared characteristic does not fail to take this very object while functioning. This is called the first line of reasoning.

items.title: Section: Food, Chariots, and Clothing — Conventional Collections That Are Cognized Yet Have No Reality of Their Own

items.zh: 道理。又於色香味觸，如是如是生起變異所安立中，施設飲食、車乘、衣服、嚴具、室宅、軍林等事。此飲食等，離色香等都無所有。此無有性，非有為攝、非無為攝，自相觀識非不緣彼境界而轉。是名第二言論道理。
items.en: Second, the reasoning that establishes conventionally designated things. With respect to form, smell, taste, and touch, in whatever way they arise and combine in transformation, one designates food and drink, chariots and carriages, clothing, ornaments, dwellings, armies, forests, and the like. These designated things, apart from form, smell, and the rest, have no existence at all — this non-existence is subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned. The consciousness that contemplates the self-characteristic does not fail to take this very object while functioning. This is called the second line of reasoning.

items.title: Section: Even Wrong Views Prove the Point — And Why Impermanence Itself Must Be an Object of Mind

items.zh: 又撥一切都無所有邪見，謂無施、無愛、亦無祠祀，廣說如前。若施、愛、祠等無性是有，即如是見應非邪見。何以故？彼如實見、如實說故。此若是無，諸邪見者緣此境界，識應不轉。是名第三言論道理。又諸行中，無常、無恒、無不變易。此諸行中，常、恒、不變無性，非有為攝、非無為攝，共相觀識非不緣此境界而轉。若緣此境識不轉者，便於諸行常、恒、不變無性之中，不能如實智慧觀察。若不觀察，應不生厭；若不生厭，應不離欲；若不離欲，應無解脫；若無解脫，應無永盡究竟涅槃。
items.en:
Third, the reasoning that establishes wrong views. There is furthermore the nihilistic view denying that anything exists at all — denying giving, denying loving support, and denying ancestral offering, as explained more fully before. If the absence of merit in giving, loving support, and offering were genuinely real, this view would not even be a wrong view, since its holder would simply be seeing and speaking truly. Yet if this is not real, and consciousness cannot function by taking this as its object, then those holding such wrong views could never have their consciousness function in this way at all. This is called the third line of reasoning.
Fourth, the reasoning that establishes impermanence. Furthermore, among conditioned things, there is no permanence, no constancy, no changelessness. This absence of permanence, constancy, and changelessness in conditioned things has no nature at all, subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned; the consciousness that contemplates this shared characteristic does not fail to take this very object while functioning.
If consciousness could not function by taking this object, one could never wisely and truly contemplate this absence of permanence, constancy, and changelessness among conditioned things. If one could not so contemplate, one could not give rise to revulsion; without revulsion, one could not become free of desire; without freedom from desire, there could be no liberation; without liberation, there could be no final, complete extinguishing in nirvāṇa.

items.zh: 若有此理，一切有情應皆究竟

blocks.text: Fascicle 52 continues the Section on Ascertainment with the four conditions, and then a careful argument: the mind can take as its object things that do not really exist.

When one mind and its factors cease without gap and the next arise, the former is the condition for the latter. Master Cháng Bǎi: the former thought must give up its seat before the next can arise; the two never occupy it together. One and the same condition is called the mental faculty, the mental sense-base, and the mental element. At the world's foremost stage, an uncontaminated mind arises without gap from a contaminated one; this condition depends on succession, not on the two minds being of one kind.
Master Cháng Bǎi: if one does not direct attention, one sees without seeing and hears without hearing. Attention rouses the mind to arise.
The field with manure and water is the condition that brings crops to completion. Master Cháng Bǎi: only with a field and the help of manure and water can seedlings ripen.
"The causal condition alone is the generative cause; the remaining three are merely instrumental causes."

subs.head: The mind can take the non-existent

blocks.text: Master Cháng Bǎi: the Sarvāstivādins hold that an object must be real; the Mahāyāna says mental consciousness can take what is not real. What the five senses take is only the existent.
The self has no nature at all, yet the consciousness contemplating its absence still takes it as object. Master Cháng Bǎi: in contemplating selflessness, one does take "self" as an object.

Food and chariots are designated upon form, smell, taste, and touch, and apart from these have no existence. Master Cháng Bǎi: say "car" and its appearance comes to mind; the mind can take a collective name without substance.

Without contemplating impermanence there is no revulsion, without revulsion no freedom from desire, without that no liberation, and without liberation no final nirvāṇa. So the mind must be able to take even this non-existent "permanence" as its object, in order to see through it.
Master Cháng Bǎi's "seeing without seeing" describes every distracted moment. Attention is a condition we can actually choose.

quiz.q: How does the treatise define the condition of immediate succession?
options: mind and mental factors arising together serve reciprocally as this condition
when these minds and mental factors have ceased without gap and those thereupon arise, the former are the condition for the latter
each phenomenon's own seed, which generates it, is this condition
the twelve internal and external sense-bases taken by mental consciousness, each in turn, are what is called the condition of immediate succession
quiz.why: The treatise defines this condition by succession: whenever these minds and mental factors have ceased without gap and those arise, the former are the condition for the latter. Master Cháng Bǎi: the mind and factors of the former thought, in ceasing, condition those of the next thought.

quiz.q: What image does Master Cháng Bǎi use to picture the condition of immediate succession?
options: the former thought must yield its seat before the next can arise
the later thought must first push the former thought aside in order to arise
the two thoughts stand side by side, supporting each other
the former thought stays in place until the later one joins it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi says the mind and factors of the former thought must give up a seat before the following mind and factors can arise; the two never occupy that place together, which is why the former's ceasing is itself the condition.

quiz.q: When these six consciousnesses serve as the condition of immediate succession for the six that follow, what name is designated?
options: manas, also called the defiled mind
the sense-base of mental objects, also called the element of phenomena
the store-consciousness, also called the consciousness holding all seeds, also called the ripening one
the mental faculty, also called the mental sense-base and the mental element
quiz.why: The treatise designates this very set the mental faculty, also the mental sense-base and the mental element. Master Cháng Bǎi: one and the same condition is named the mental faculty under the six faculties, the mental sense-base under the twelve bases, and the mental element under the eighteen elements.

quiz.q: Can the condition of immediate succession span contaminated and uncontaminated minds? When does Master Cháng Bǎi say this happens?
options: yes: from the world's foremost stage one moment enters the path of seeing, an uncontaminated mind following a contaminated one without gap
no: the contaminated leads only to the contaminated and the uncontaminated only to the uncontaminated, and a gap of some time is needed before any change between them
yes, but only at buddhahood does a contaminated mind lead to an uncontaminated one
yes, but only on emerging from the attainment of cessation
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: when practice reaches the world's foremost stage, in a single moment one enters the path of seeing, and an uncontaminated mind arises without gap from a contaminated one. So this condition depends on succession, not on the two minds being of one kind.

quiz.q: How do the objects of the five sense-consciousnesses and of mental consciousness differ as condition of the perceived object?
options: the five take form and the rest of the five objects in order; mental consciousness takes all twelve internal and external sense-bases
the five take the five inner bases; mental consciousness takes the five outer objects
the five and mental consciousness alike take all twelve sense-bases
the five take form and the rest of the five objects in order; mental consciousness takes only what is subsumed under the sense-base of mental objects
quiz.why: The treatise assigns the five objects, each in its order, to the five sense-consciousnesses, and all twelve internal and external sense-bases to mental consciousness. Master Cháng Bǎi spells out the five: form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.

quiz.q: Under the inducing dominant condition, how does Master Cháng Bǎi stress the importance of attention?
options: attention is the co-arising dominant condition of eye-consciousness and the rest; without it the eye faculty cannot see
attention exists only in meditation; daily consciousness does not need it
without attention one sees without seeing and hears without hearing; attention rouses the mind to arise
attention is a force of the outer object drawing the mind towards it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: if one does not direct attention towards seeing or hearing, one sees without seeing and hears without hearing; so the mental factor of attention matters greatly, for it rouses one's own mind to arise. Attention is thus the inducing condition, not the eye faculty, which is the co-arising condition.

quiz.q: A field together with manure and water is which dominant condition for crops and seedlings?
options: the dominant condition bringing a result to completion
the dominant condition that was previously accomplished before
the dominant condition of skilled craft
the mutual dominant condition
quiz.why: The treatise names the field with manure and water as the condition bringing crops to completion. Master Cháng Bǎi: only with a field and the aid of manure and water can seedlings and crops ripen. Skilled craft, by contrast, concerns craft-knowledge and its worldly activity.

quiz.q: How do the four conditions map onto the two causes?
options: the causal and immediately succeeding conditions are generative causes; the other two are merely instrumental causes
the dominant condition is generative; the other three are instrumental
all four are generative; instrumental causes are established apart from them
the causal condition alone is the generative cause; the other three are merely instrumental causes
quiz.why: The treatise says the causal condition alone is the generative cause in relation to what is produced, and the remaining three should be known as merely instrumental causes. Master Cháng Bǎi: the generative cause is the principal condition, the instrumental cause a secondary one.

quiz.q: What position stands behind the objection to "past and future conditioned phenomena serve as condition giving rise to mental consciousness"?
options: Sautrāntikas hold that past and future are definitely real; the Mahāyāna says that only the present thought is empty of reality
outsiders hold that mind comes from a soul; the Dharma says mind arises without cause
Sarvāstivādins hold that nothing exists; the Mahāyāna says past and future are real
Sarvāstivādins hold that an object must be real; the Mahāyāna says mental consciousness can take what is not real
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the Sarvāstivādins of the Śrāvaka Vehicle maintain that an object must be real, while the Mahāyāna says what mental consciousness takes need not be real; it can take what lacks reality as object, and this is called the meaning of mind taking the non-existent.

quiz.q: Why did the Blessed One provisionally apply the name "phenomena" to the object of mental consciousness?
options: because the sense-base of mental objects is real, just like the five objects
because the five also take past and future, the name applies to all
because mental consciousness takes hold of what the five sense-consciousnesses cannot engage, the name is provisionally applied
because phenomena is another name for mental factors, which always accompany mind
quiz.why: The treatise answers that mental consciousness can take hold of what the five sense-consciousness bodies cannot engage, and so the Blessed One provisionally applied the name. Master Cháng Bǎi: what the five take is only the existent, whereas what mental consciousness takes is both the existent and the non-existent.

quiz.q: How does the first line of reasoning, establishing selflessness, prove that consciousness can take the non-existent?
options: this self is conditioned, so the contemplating consciousness can take it
this self is unconditioned, so only uncontaminated wisdom can take it
this self has no nature, subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, yet the consciousness contemplating the shared characteristic functions on it
this self has no nature, subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, so the consciousness contemplating the shared characteristic functions on no object at all
quiz.why: The self has no nature and falls under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, yet the consciousness contemplating this shared characteristic does not fail to take it as object. Master Cháng Bǎi: in cultivating contemplation of selflessness, one does indeed take selflessness as the object of examination.

quiz.q: What does the second reasoning, on food, chariots, and the like, set out to show?
options: these things are real entities combined from form, smell, taste, and touch, which is why the consciousness contemplating the self-characteristic can function on them
these things are unconditioned, existing apart from form and smell
these things are seeds that generate form, smell, taste, and touch
apart from form, smell, and the rest these things are nothing, yet the consciousness contemplating the self-characteristic functions on them
quiz.why: The treatise says food, chariots, and the like are designated upon form, smell, taste, and touch, and apart from these have no existence. Master Cháng Bǎi: apart from form, smell, taste, and touch they have no reality at all. Yet consciousness takes them, which supports the claim that mind can take the non-existent.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi use the example of "a car" to support the claim?
options: when one says "car" its image appears; a collective name has no substance yet mind takes it, proving mind takes the non-existent
a car is assembled from parts, so it has real substance
when a car is not before one's eyes, mental consciousness cannot take it
only the five can take a car; mind takes only its name
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: a car itself is subsumed under neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, yet when one says "car" its appearance comes to mind. So mental consciousness can take a collective name without substance, which proves the meaning of mind taking the non-existent.

quiz.q: If consciousness could not take the absence of permanence as its object, what does the treatise conclude?
options: contemplation remains, but it yields only revulsion, not freedom from desire
no contemplation, yet one could still gain liberation through absorption
conditioned things would be permanent, so all beings would already be in nirvāṇa
no contemplation, hence no revulsion, no freedom from desire, no liberation, no final nirvāṇa
quiz.why: The treatise runs the chain: without such contemplation no revulsion, without revulsion no freedom from desire, without that no liberation, and without liberation no final nirvāṇa. Master Cháng Bǎi: if mental consciousness could not take the non-existent "permanence," there could be no concept of impermanence.
